name: Anti-authoritarianism
summary: Anti-authoritarianism opposes unquestioning obedience and the exercise of illegitimate, unaccountable power, whether by governments, employers, teachers or parents. The defining sources use the name in several ways: for people who test an authority's legitimacy and resist it if it fails; for the nonviolent, humanist 'revolution of dignity' of the East European dissidents against communist rule; and for an anti-capitalist, anti-fascist left that treats authoritarianism as bound up with capitalism, patriarchy and colonialism. A fourth, psychological sense (a personality trait or construct) describes people and takes no political position.

human-caused-global-warming.rationale: Von Redecker, "What time is it?", section "Neoliberalism and the destruction of future time": climate warming and mass extinction come from extractivism and fossil capitalism, "most of all fossil fuels", with its "ecocidal effects" known. She does not use the phrase 'main cause' of warming, so +1.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century", section "Reclaiming futures": global capitalism "has been intimately interwoven with patriarchy, racism, and colonialism"; section "Decentering anti-authoritarianism": the editors name the forms "together, as well as ... recognize our many struggles against them as one".

one-party-rule.rationale: Witoszek, Introduction (p. 15): the humanist outliers "unmasked the evil of Bolshevism and built a microcosm of democracy within the walls of an authoritarian state"; ch. 4 (p. 102) quotes Michnik on "the dictatorship of the party". Beyond Molotovs's introduction treats authoritarian rule as the thing to defeat.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century": "democracy is about equality and collective decision-making", and the book presents strategies that propose "more democratic ways of being together"; von Redecker ("What time is it?", "Revolution for life") lists "New forms of democratic self-organization" among anti-authoritarian struggles. Direct participation in daily decisions is implied by these passages rather than stated as a programme, so +1.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Split between strands. Witoszek (Introduction, pp. 4-5, and ch. 1) adopts the finding that "non-violent civil resistance remains the best strategy" and that movements that opt for violence "often unleash terrible destruction and bloodshed"; the dissidents' revolution of dignity used "peaceful and pragmatic means" (Introduction, p. 15). Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century", section "Beyond Molotovs" paragraph, says a wide variety of initiatives is needed, "from classical antifascist organizing ... to militant struggle against oppressive regimes", and does not disregard those forms. Neither strand states a general ban or a general endorsement.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century", section "Reclaiming futures": "Capitalism is based on the exploitation of the many by the few". The wording is about capitalism in general rather than profit on owned businesses specifically, hence +1.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Witoszek's thesis is that anti-authoritarian revolutions like 1989 succeeded through a nonviolent "revolution of dignity" (Introduction, blurb and pp. 4-5; ch. 1 p. 39 on "peaceful anti-authoritarian revolution"), while Michnik, quoted in ch. 4 ("Three weddings and a funeral?", p. 102), rejects overthrow by force. Von Redecker's essay "What time is it?" (section "Revolution for life") calls anti-authoritarianism a radical political force. Revolution is endorsed, so +1, with the means limited in Witoszek's strand.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century", section "Anti-authoritarian strategies through the kaleidoscope": authoritarianism works by "silencing those who are inconvenient", and the strategies it presents "make visible what has been suppressed". Witoszek (ch. 1, pp. 36-37) describes the dissidents' opposition to a system that said "If you have to speak, don't write".

total-state.rationale: Witoszek, ch. 1 "The second renaissance in 20th-century Europe", pp. 36-37: Solidarność's cultivation of excellence was "a defence against the totalitarian bulldozer wiping out human autonomy" and individuality, an "exhausting, relentless opposition" to a system that said "Don't think".

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Witoszek, Introduction (p. 15) and ch. 1 (pp. 38-40): the dissidents' Poland was a "theatre of brown and red totalitarianism"; they unmasked "the evil of Bolshevism"; she speaks of "brown and red totalitarianism" together. She notes that the term fits communist Poland only loosely in doctrinal terms. Beyond Molotovs does not address communist states in this way.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Beyond Molotovs, editors' introduction "Beyond Authoritarianism: For an Anti-Fascism of the 21st Century", section "Reclaiming futures": capitalism brings "an ever-greater concentration of wealth and power to the detriment of our well-being and capacity to determine the course of our own lives", and democratic rights must be defended against the dominant classes; later "redistribute rather than concentrate wealth" (section "An anti-fascism for the 21st century"). Stated for capitalism's wealth and power together, so +1.

missingStatements.text: People should not obey an authority without first judging whether it is legitimate.
missingStatements.rationale: Levine defines anti-authoritarians as people who give no unquestioning obedience and instead assess an authority's legitimacy before resisting it if it fails; he sets this against the authoritarian demand for blind submission.

quotes.text: anti-authoritarians reject—for themselves and for others—an unquestioning obedience to authority, and they believe in challenging and resisting illegitimate authority.
quotes.where: Excerpt from Resisting Illegitimate Authority, first paragraph

quotes.text: anti-authoritarian means opposing authoritarians, authoritarianism, and illegitimate authority.
quotes.where: Curious 'Anti-Authoritarian' Definitions and Divides, section on anti-authority

scope: Profiled strands, as the defining sources present them: (1) Bruce E. Levine's account of anti-authoritarians as people who resist illegitimate authority rather than all authority (s6, s7, s8); (2) Nina Witoszek's 'The Origins of Anti-Authoritarianism' (2019), on the nonviolent humanist 'revolution of dignity' of the Polish and East European dissidents and Solidarity (s3); (3) the editors' introduction and the framing essays by Eva von Redecker, Gustavo Robles, Lorena Zárate and Firoozeh Farvardin in 'Beyond Molotovs: A Visual Handbook of Anti-Authoritarian Strategies' (2024), the anti-capitalist, anti-fascist left (s4); (4) William Kreml's 'The Anti-Authoritarian Personality' (1977), used only for its psychological construct, which gives no political answers (s5). Positions are taken only where these authors speak in their own voice; the contributors' case-study chapters in Beyond Molotovs and the dissidents quoted by Witoszek are not counted as the strand's position unless the author adopts them. Excluded: anarchism proper (an anti-state doctrine with its own profile, though anarchists use the label and Levine writes for anarchist publishers), the Kaczynski/primitivist 'Industrial Society and Its Future' pamphlet, and the Kasama/KSL anarchist collections, which none of the defining sources above treats as the ideology's own texts.

the anti-authoritarian AK Press invited me to write a book for them, and I thought that the time was right for Resisting Illegitimate Authority
